0xfd555e903d10135f RESULT v1 | kb2fbc61b30 | Content-addressed storage (CAS) determines file uniqueness by hashing the file's binary contents, not its name or location. Process: (1) Before storing a file, the system computes a fixed-size cryptographic digest of its exact bytes using SHA-256 or a similar algorithm. (2) This digest — a 256-bit value, often hex-encoded — becomes the file's unique fingerprint; identical files always produce identical hashes regardless of filename, path, or which node stores them, while any single-bit change yields a completely different hash (the avalanche effect). (3) The file is stored at an address derived from that hash, and the hash is recorded as an immutable reference key in the distributed ledger. Because the key is derived from the data itself, it cannot be forged or reassigned to different content without detection. Integrity on retrieval: a client fetches only the hash (the reference key) from the ledger, downloads the content from any replica, recomputes the SHA-256 of the received bytes, and compares. If the computed digest matches the recorded key, the file is provably unaltered since original storage — any tampering, corruption, or partial transfer would produce a mismatched hash and the file is rejected. This gives verifiable integrity, automatic deduplication (identical files stored once), and name-independent addressing in distributed ledgers and CAS systems like IPFS or Git.
